I've managed software projects for almost twenty years, and I can tell you exactly how most of them fail. It isn't one big mistake. It's a hundred small requests. Someone asks for one extra report. Then a new button. Then a version for the sales team, just a small one. Every request sounds reasonable on its own, and nobody wants to say no in a meeting. Six months later, the project is twice as big, the budget is the same, and everyone is angry. We call it scope creep. The cure is boring, but it works. Before we start, we write down what the project includes, and, just as important, what it doesn't include. We define the words that people will argue about later, like finished, or tested, or live. And when a new request comes in, we don't say no. We say, that's outside the current scope, so let's estimate it as a change. People are surprisingly happy with that answer.

I've been renovating kitchens for twenty-five years, and the most expensive word in my business is everything. A client says, I want you to do everything. Does that include the floor? The lights? Moving the sink to the other wall? So I never start a job without a one-page scope of work. It lists what's included, item by item, and then it lists what's excluded, because that's the part people forget. Painting the living room is excluded, even if the paint is already in the house. I also define finished. For me, finished means the kitchen works and has been cleaned, not that every cabinet handle is the one you saw online last week. My clients sometimes think the paper is a little cold. But when we disagree in the third week, and we always disagree in the third week, nobody has to remember what anybody said. We just read the page together, and we usually agree in five minutes.
